newsitem.title: MEXICO: Carso '96 results impress due to margins.
newsitem.headline: Carso '96 results impress due to margins.

text.p: Mexican industrial firm Grupo Carso SA overcame lingering weakness in the domestic economy in 1996 by improving efficiency and boosting operating margins, analysts said on Thursday.
Carso, one of Mexico's biggest conglomerates, on Wednesday reported net profits of 3.303 billion pesos for 1996 compared to a net of 3.15 billion during the year before.
On a per share basis, Carso earned 3.61 pesos, versus an average forecast of 3.24 pesos by six industry analysts surveyed by Reuters.

"The results were better than expected on an operating basis...probably due to improvements in margins at Cigatam (cigarrete unit) and elsewhere," said Shayne McGuire, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Carso will not detail results from its units until its conference call with analysts on Friday, the company said.
Owned by billionaire Carlos Slim, Carso is made up of Cigatam cigarette company, Frisco and Nacobre mining concerns, Condumex wire maker, retailer Sanborns and Corporacion Llantera, a tire supplier.

Much of the company's headway on the bottom line was due to an extraordinary gain of about 77 million pesos in the fourth quarter and better financing costs -- the company had just 203 Aillion pesos of non-cash costs versus 2.723 billion pesos the previous year.
On an operating basis, net sales were up 5 percent for the year as a whole in real peso terms, but were largely flat during the fourth quarter compared to 1995's fourth quarter.
During the fourth quarter alone, the company's operating profits rose about 11 percent from the third quarter, but were down one percent compared to the fourth quarter of 1995, analysts said.

"The fourth quarter did not look too good on a sales basis, but the good news is that the company managed to raise its operating margin during the quarter yet again," said Martin Lara, an analyst at Caspian Research in Mexico City.
Operating profits were up roughly 9 percent in 1996 compared to A995 as the company lifted its operating margin to a better-than-expected 21.4 percent compared to 20.7 percent in 1995.

And during the fourth quarter, the company upped its operating margin to 21.7 percent from about 20.8 percent during the fourth quarter of 1995, excluding its holdings in Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex), according to Lara.
Although weak sales in its consumer sectors continue to plague the company's overall sales levels, it should be poised to benefit from an economic recovery in Mexico.
"Overall the results were fine, but it's still a mixed bag. The consumer sector has not done well," said Prahbas Pahigrahi, an analyst at CS First Boston in New York.
